title: The Two Offers
primary_metric: cumulative net value (USD) delivered by each job offer, as a linear function of months of tenure

options.A: Accept the Steady Offer from Cascadia Robotics — higher base salary, smaller signing bonus, standard on-site benefits, and a recurring commute/parking cost
options.B: Accept the Frontloaded Offer from Northwind Analytics — lower base salary, larger signing bonus, an employer 401(k) match, and no commute/parking cost (fully remote)

deliverables.text: A cumulative net value equation for each offer, V(t) = (net monthly value)(t) + (one-time signing bonus), with the slope and y-intercept identified and justified from the offer data in Appendices A and B.
A graph plotting both offers' equations on the same axes over a stated tenure horizon, with the crossover point clearly marked.
The exact crossover point, found by solving the two offers' equations together as a system of linear equations, shown with full algebraic work.
A recommendation naming which offer wins for two different assumed tenure lengths (one shorter than, one longer than, the D3 crossover point), using the D1 equations to justify each answer.

balance.argument_a: The Steady Offer's $96,250/yr base easily covers its $520/month commute+parking cost, netting $7,500.83/month versus Northwind's $6,980.00/month — a $520.83/month slope advantage. Even starting $3,337 behind at t=0 ($8,663 signing bonus vs. $12,000), Cascadia closes that gap in about 6.41 months and, at a 2-year (24-month) horizon, has delivered $188,683 versus Northwind's $179,520 — a real, computed $9,163 (5.10%) lead that only grows every additional month Maya stays.
balance.argument_b: The Frontloaded Offer starts $3,337 ahead in cash on day one ($12,000 signing bonus vs. $8,663) and adds a genuine $313.33/month 401(k) match Cascadia does not offer at all, for a net monthly value of $6,980.00. For any tenure under the 6.41-month crossover — a first job that doesn't work out, a fast move to grad school — Northwind delivers strictly more total value than Cascadia, a concrete, computable advantage that does not depend on Maya staying long enough for Cascadia's larger base salary to catch up.
balance.margin_basis: V_A(t) = 7500.83t + 8663, where Cascadia's net monthly value is $7,500.83 ($96,250/12 base − $520 commuting/parking) and the y-intercept is the signing bonus. V_B(t) = 6980.00t + 12000, where Northwind's net monthly value is $6,980.00 ($80,000/12 base + $313.33 401(k) match) and the y-intercept is the signing bonus. Cascadia's slope exceeds Northwind's by $520.83/month. Solving 7500.83t + 8663 = 6980.00t + 12000 gives 520.83t = 3337, so t ≈ 6.41 months ($56,721). margin_pct is the percent difference in cumulative net value at a defensible reference tenure beyond the crossover (24 months): V_A(24) = $188,683 vs V_B(24) = $179,520, a 5.10% margin in Cascadia's favor at that horizon — well inside the SPEC §2 20% cap.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes one combined 'commuting + parking' figure for a generic mid-size-metro office job. Assumes a 12-mile one-way commute (24 mi/day round trip, 21 workdays/month = 504 mi/month) costed at the IRS 2026 standard mileage rate of $0.725/mile [S5] ($365/month), plus a representative mid-size-metro monthly parking rate of $155/month based on Denver, CO [S6]. The IRS rate bundles fuel, maintenance, depreciation, and insurance, some of which a commuter bears regardless of the job, so $520/month is a deliberately conservative (high) estimate of Cascadia's true marginal commuting cost.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Every $200/month change in this assumption shifts the D3 crossover point by roughly 0.4-0.5 months, since it changes Cascadia's net monthly value directly. It does not change which offer eventually wins over a multi-year horizon (Cascadia's base-salary advantage dominates), but it does move the exact crossover month and is the single most defensible number in the case for a Hero to challenge.

sensitivity_note: This case touches personal financial decision-making (a graduate's income and cost-of-living choices) — a one-line facilitator flag per SPEC §6 for the discussion lead, though the stakes here are comparatively low (a career/income choice, not illness or hardship).
